To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). # Project Kestrel: Seller Position Review (Buyer Perspective)

## Bottom line

The Seller's package is not a fair or balanced allocation for a 100% buyer acquiring a business with several known, quantified exposures. Read together, the general disclosure of the data room (Schedule 7 / DL 1.1-1.2), the anti-sandbagging clause (8.3), and the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance language (9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5) mean that **the Buyer would have almost no warranty recourse for any matter in the data room, including the ten issues the Seller has already identified.** The Seller has disclosed the problems and then removed the Buyer's ability to claim for them.

Our first priority should be specific indemnities, price adjustments, and conditions for the known issues. Warranty negotiation is secondary to that.

I have reviewed only the Seller's summary positions and the disclosure letter. I have not seen the full SPA draft, the underlying data room documents (DD-002 to DD-012), or the Buyer's own valuation. The points below are based on the descriptions provided and should be checked against the actual clause wording and verified by NSW counsel and, where relevant, tax and privacy specialists.

---

## Part A: Where the Seller departs from Buyer interests

### A1. Risk architecture (the structural problems)

**1. General disclosure of the entire data room (DL 1.1, 1.2; Schedule 7)**
The Seller discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room and public registers. This is effectively a fair-disclosure override of every warranty. The Buyer would be deemed to have accepted anything in thousands of pages, without identifying it against a specific warranty. This is the most dangerous clause in the package.
*Push back:* Disclosure must be specific, fair, and against a named warranty. Data room general disclosure should be deleted. Reference to the data room should be limited to specific documents identified in a schedule, with the relevant facts stated.

**2. Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging (cl 8.3)**
The Buyer loses any claim for matters it "had knowledge" of or that were "discoverable" from the data room or public records. Combined with point 1, this removes recourse for everything in the data room. "Discoverable" is also an uncertain standard that invites dispute. Under NSW law, the position on knowledge and warranty claims depends heavily on express wording, so the Seller's inclusion of this clause matters.
*Push back:* Delete cl 8.3 and insert an express pro-sandbagging clause (the Buyer may claim regardless of its knowledge). Known issues should instead be addressed by specific indemnities (see Part B).

**3. General cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m) (cl 12.1)**
A 20% cap on general warranties, combined with the other limits below, leaves the Buyer with little protection on a AUD 24m acquisition, especially given the scale of the known exposures (see the revenue, debt and privacy items).
*Push back:* Open at a materially higher general cap (we suggest at least 30-50% of price as a starting position, with a fallback we set after valuation work), and a cap equal to the purchase price for title, capacity, and tax warranties and for the specific indemnities.

**4. Thresholds (cl 12.2)**
- The **AUD 25,000 de minimis** excludes individual claims below that amount entirely, even if they are part of a larger pattern.
- The **AUD 250,000 basket** operates as a deductible: the Buyer absorbs the first AUD 250k of losses, and only the excess is recoverable. On a deal of this size, that is a significant retention.
*Push back:* Reduce the de minimis (ideally to AUD 10k or less) and require that related claims be aggregated. Replace the deductible basket with a **tipping basket** (once the threshold is crossed, all losses from the first dollar are recoverable). Clarify whether de minimis claims count towards the basket, which the Seller's text does not state.

**5. Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13)**
- General warranty claims must be notified within 18 months. That is short for an acquisition where tax returns and privacy issues may surface later.
- The Seller proposes that "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims". This would apply the 18-month period to title, capacity, and tax claims.
*Push back:* General warranties should be at least 24-36 months. Tax claims should run to at least the ATO's standard amendment period (generally four years after the relevant assessment is issued) or longer. Title, capacity, and fundamental warranties should run for the statutory or contractual maximum. Clarify the difference between notification periods and the time to commence proceedings. Under the *Limitation Act 1969* (NSW) the default period for contract claims is generally six years, and the contract should not shorten the Buyer's ability to sue on claims it has properly notified.

**6. Title and capacity subject to general caps and time limits (Fundamental / Title)**
The Seller's "administrative simplicity" rationale is not a commercial reason. Title and capacity warranties go to whether the Buyer actually gets what it is paying for. Subjecting them to a 20% cap and 18-month limit is unacceptable.
*Push back:* Title, capacity, and authority warranties should be uncapped (or capped at price), outside the basket, and survive for the longest period.

**7. Exclusive remedy, non-reliance, and limitations applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)**
These provisions would apply to fraud and to the Buyer's specific indemnities. An exclusive-remedy clause that catches fraud is problematic. Non-reliance clauses are generally enforceable between commercial parties, but their effect on misleading or deceptive conduct claims under the Australian Consumer Law (s 18) should be checked with NSW counsel. A broad non-reliance clause should not be able to protect the Seller against its own fraud.
*Push back:* Carve out fraud, title, capacity, tax, and specific indemnities from all limitations, the exclusive-remedy clause, and non-reliance. Non-reliance should be limited to statements outside the SPA and should not qualify the warranties or the Seller's disclosure of its own representations.

**8. Tax and IP warranty positions "settled under the general regime" (Tax / IP)**
Treating tax and IP as part of the general regime, with its caps and time limits, leaves the Buyer exposed to pre-Completion tax liabilities that may not crystallise for years.
*Push back:* Include a pre-Completion tax indemnity, uncapped or capped at price, with a survival period matching the ATO amendment period. Give IP title and non-infringement warranties the same treatment as fundamental warranties.

### A2. Specific issues

**9. Bluefen change-control consent (cl 3 / 6.3; DL 2)**
Bluefen represents about AUD 3.6m (approximately 30%) of FY26 revenue. The consent has not been obtained, and the conditions in cl 11.3 have not been shown as satisfied. The Seller proposes to treat consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent, with a "reasonable endeavours" obligation. This is a weak position for the following reasons:
- Delivery of consent does not, on its own, satisfy the conditions in cl 11.3.
- "Reasonable endeavours" gives the Seller little real obligation to procure consent, and the Buyer has no control over Bluefen.
- If the Bluefen contract terminates or is varied on change of control, the business value could fall materially.

*Push back:* Make the Bluefen consent, together with satisfaction of the cl 11.3 conditions, an express condition precedent in a form the Buyer approves. The Buyer should have the right to terminate if it is not received by a long-stop date. Failing that, an earn-out, deferred consideration, or specific indemnity for lost Bluefen revenue should apply. The Buyer should not be able to waive the condition without a specific price or indemnity arrangement.

**10. Riverlark Bank facility (cl 2 / 7; DL 3)**
The facility has about AUD 3.2m outstanding and has not been repaid. The Seller proposes a discharge "following Completion". The deal is debt-free and cash-free, so this debt should reduce the price at Completion, not be left for post-Completion administration. A post-Completion release leaves the Buyer owning a company with a secured lender still holding security over its assets, with change-of-control provisions (cl 8.1) potentially triggered.
*Push back:* Require a payoff letter and a discharge of security (including PPSR removals) to be delivered at Completion. The payoff amount must be deducted from the price in the funds flow. Riverlark should be treated as "Closing Indebtedness" in the price definition.

**11. Ironquay Development Studio / IP (cl 11.1; DL 4)**
The Seller calls the existing indemnity adequate, but it is limited to the SOW3 payment. Project Materials transfer only on payment of every SOW3 fee (DD-004 cl 7.3). AUD 180,000 is recorded as open (DD-010) and there is no evidence of payment or of a confirmatory assignment. Until payment is made and assignment is delivered, the Company may not own the IP it is relying on. The indemnity as drafted does not cover this.
*Push back:* Require either (a) payment of the open amount before Completion, treated as debt-like and deducted from price, or (b) a Seller-funded settlement with Ironquay and an executed confirmatory assignment as a condition precedent. Add a specific, uncapped IP title indemnity covering any claim that the Company does not own or lacks rights to the Project Materials.

**12. Employee Completion bonuses, AUD 420,000 (DD-005; DL 5)**
These bonuses are conditional, but they are excluded from the draft Completion funds flow, and the disclosure does not say whether payroll tax, superannuation, or other on-costs apply. Superannuation guarantee alone would add a material amount on top of the AUD 420k (verify the current SG rate with tax advisers). These are transaction-related liabilities that the Buyer would inherit.
*Push back:* Treat the bonuses and all related employer on-costs (including payroll tax and superannuation) as debt-like or transaction-related items deducted from the price. Require the Seller to bear the cost of any bonus triggered by Completion, and make the Company's payment obligations clear in the funds flow.

**13. Privacy and data export incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6; DD-006; DL 6)**
This is more serious than the Seller's "preliminary operational matter" framing. The export may contain about 1,240 records with names, business emails, roles, and activity timestamps. That is personal information. The Seller says it does not yet know whether unauthorised access occurred or whether notification is required. Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must carry out a reasonable assessment within 30 days, and must notify if serious harm is likely. The Company's assessment timing and outcome therefore matter, and it may already be running out of time.
*Push back:* Before signing, require a completed forensic assessment and a privacy compliance review. Add a specific indemnity covering investigation costs, notification costs, remediation, third-party claims, and regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully recoverable. The indemnity should be uncapped (or capped at price) and secured by an escrow or retention. Confirm whether the Company has cyber or privacy insurance and whether the Buyer can benefit from it.

**14. Office lease (cl ? / DL 7)**
The lease has a notification obligation, and the disclosure does not say whether the share sale requires landlord consent. Many commercial leases deem a change of control to be an assignment.
*Push back:* Obtain a legal review of the lease. If consent is required, make it a condition precedent. If not, obtain landlord confirmation that the share sale does not require consent and does not trigger default.

**15. Supplier renewals, AUD 330,000 (DD-008 / DD-011; DL 8)**
The Seller calls these "ordinary-course operating costs", but the disclosure says three renewals of AUD 110,000 each, read together, could be a commitment that is not ordinary course, prepaid, or unavoidable. The disclosure does not say whether they are terminable or accrued.
*Push back:* Treat any renewal commitments that are outside ordinary course, accrued, prepaid, or not terminable on short notice as debt-like items or deduct them from price. Require that no new supplier commitments be entered into after signing without Buyer consent.

**16. Mossvale assignment restriction (DL 9)**
The disclosure does not confirm that the share sale does not trigger the restriction.
*Push back:* Require a legal opinion or counterparty confirmation that no consent is needed for a share sale. If consent is needed, make it a condition precedent.

**17. Title (DL 10 / Share register)**
The Seller relies on the share register at DD-012 as evidence of title. The register alone does not establish good title, and the Buyer has not completed its own verification.
*Push back:* The Buyer should carry out its own title verification (ASIC company searches, original share certificates, a register of members inspection, and PPSR searches). Require a title warranty and fundamental warranty, uncapped or capped at price, with the Seller covering any title defect.

**18. Funds flow and price mechanics**
The funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics", but it excludes the bonuses, does not clearly show the Riverlark payoff, and does not clearly reflect debt-like items. For a debt-free, cash-free deal, the price adjustment mechanism (completion accounts, locked box, or price adjustment) needs to be clear.
*Push back:* Require a full, reconciled funds flow with every debt-like item, the Riverlark payoff, and a defined net debt and working capital mechanism. Confirm whether the deal is completion accounts or locked box, and confirm the leakage protections if it is locked box.

**19. Disclosure letter drafting issues**
Schedule numbering appears inconsistent (for example, the general disclosure is in Schedule 7 but the incident is in Schedule 6, and clause references are cross-referenced in different places). The DL also states that the Seller "does NOT" characterise several matters as confirmed (privacy incident, lease, Mossvale), which is helpful for the Buyer's argument that those matters are not disclosed as resolved.
*Push back:* Conform the schedule numbering and cross-references, and ensure that no general or non-admission language undermines the specific warranties.

---

## Part B: Recommendations summary

| # | Issue | Seller position | Buyer ask | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Data room general disclosure | All data room facts disclosed | Delete; specific disclosure only | Critical |
| 2 | Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3) | No claims for known or discoverable matters | Delete; express pro-sandbagging clause | Critical |
| 3 | Specific indemnities for the 10 known issues | None | Add specific indemnities outside cap/basket, with escrow or retention | Critical |
| 4 | General warranty cap | 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Higher (open at 30-50%) | High |
| 5 | Title, capacity, tax, fundamental | General regime | Cap at price; longer survival; outside basket | Critical |
| 6 | Basket | Deductible at AUD 250k | Tipping basket; de minimis at or below AUD 10k with aggregation | High |
| 7 | Time limits | 18 months for all claims | General 24-36 months; tax to ATO amendment period (4+ years); title longer | High |
| 8 | Exclusive remedy / non-reliance / limitations | Apply to all claims | Carve out fraud, title, tax, specific indemnities | Critical |
| 9 | Bluefen consent | Reasonable endeavours; deemed satisfied on consent | CP with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied; long-stop termination; price protection | Critical |
| 10 | Riverlark debt | Discharge after Completion | Payoff letter and discharge at Completion; deduct from price | Critical |
| 11 | Ironquay IP / AUD 180k | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment | Pay pre-Completion or CP with confirmatory assignment; uncapped IP title indemnity | Critical |
| 12 | Bonuses AUD 420k + on-costs | Not in funds flow | Debt-like item; deduct from price | Critical |
| 13 | Privacy incident | "Preliminary" | Forensic report pre-signing; specific indemnity with escrow | Critical |
| 14 | Office lease | Notification only | Legal review; consent CP or landlord confirmation | High |
| 15 | Supplier renewals AUD 330k | Ordinary course | Confirm nature; debt-like or price deduction for non-ordinary commitments | High |
| 16 | Mossvale | Not stated | Confirm no consent needed or make CP | Medium |
| 17 | Title verification | Share register | Independent ASIC, certificate, PPSR checks; title warranty uncapped | High |
| 18 | Funds flow / price mechanism | "Agreed" | Reconciled funds flow; defined debt and working capital | High |
| 19 | DL drafting | Inconsistent cross-references | Conform numbering and cross-references | Low |

---

## Suggested next steps

1. **Quantify the known exposures** before the mark-up goes back: Bluefen revenue at risk and its valuation impact, Riverlark payoff, Ironquay AUD 180k, bonuses plus on-costs, supplier commitments, and privacy investigation and penalty range. These numbers drive the price adjustment and the size of the specific indemnities and escrow.
2. **Commission the privacy assessment now.** The 30-day NDB assessment clock may already be running.
3. **Insist on the full SPA draft and the data room documents** (DD-002 to DD-012) so we can check clause wording against the summaries. Several of the Seller's positions are described in summary form only.
4. **Engage NSW counsel** on the non-reliance and misleading-conduct interaction, the limitation periods, and the enforceability of the anti-sandbagging and general disclosure drafting.
5. **Engage tax advisers** on the pre-Completion tax indemnity, the superannuation and payroll tax on the bonuses, and the survival period.

*Push back:* Require either (a) payment of the open amount before Completion, treated as debt-like and deducted from price, or (b) a Seller-funded settlement with Ironquay and an executed confirmatory assignment as a condition precedent. Add a specific, uncapped IP title indemnity covering any claim that the Company does not own or lacks rights to the Project Materials.

**12. Employee Completion bonuses, AUD 420,000 (DD-005; DL 5)**
These bonuses are conditional, but they are excluded from the draft Completion funds flow, and the disclosure does not say whether payroll tax, superannuation, or other on-costs apply. Superannuation guarantee alone would add a material amount on top of the AUD 420k (verify the current SG rate with tax advisers). These are transaction-related liabilities that the Buyer would inherit.
*Push back:* Treat the bonuses and all related employer on-costs (including payroll tax and superannuation) as debt-like or transaction-related items deducted from the price. Require the Seller to bear the cost of any bonus triggered by Completion, and make the Company's payment obligations clear in the funds flow.

**13. Privacy and data export incident (cl 4.6 / Sch 6; DD-006; DL 6)**
This is more serious than the Seller's "preliminary operational matter" framing. The export may contain about 1,240 records with names, business emails, roles, and activity timestamps. That is personal information. The Seller says it does not yet know whether unauthorised access occurred or whether notification is required. Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must carry out a reasonable assessment within 30 days, and must notify if serious harm is likely. The Company's assessment timing and outcome therefore matter, and it may already be running out of time.
*Push back:* Before signing, require a completed forensic assessment and a privacy compliance review. Add a specific indemnity covering investigation costs, notification costs, remediation, third-party claims, and regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully recoverable. The indemnity should be uncapped (or capped at price) and secured by an escrow or retention. Confirm whether the Company has cyber or privacy insurance and whether the Buyer can benefit from it.

**14. Office lease (cl ? / DL 7)**
The lease has a notification obligation, and the disclosure does not say whether the share sale requires landlord consent. Many commercial leases deem a change of control to be an assignment.
*Push back:* Obtain a legal review of the lease. If consent is required, make it a condition precedent. If not, obtain landlord confirmation that the share sale does not require consent and does not trigger default.

**15. Supplier renewals, AUD 330,000 (DD-008 / DD-011; DL 8)**
The Seller calls these "ordinary-course operating costs", but the disclosure says three renewals of AUD 110,000 each, read together, could be a commitment that is not ordinary course, prepaid, or unavoidable. The disclosure does not say whether they are terminable or accrued.
*Push back:* Treat any renewal commitments that are outside ordinary course, accrued, prepaid, or not terminable on short notice as debt-like items or deduct them from price. Require that no new supplier commitments be entered into after signing without Buyer consent.

**16. Mossvale assignment restriction (DL 9)**
The disclosure does not confirm that the share sale does not trigger the restriction.
*Push back:* Require a legal opinion or counterparty confirmation that no consent is needed for a share sale. If consent is needed, make it a condition precedent.

**17. Title (DL 10 / Share register)**
The Seller relies on the share register at DD-012 as evidence of title. The register alone does not establish good title, and the Buyer has not completed its own verification.
*Push back:* The Buyer should carry out its own title verification (ASIC company searches, original share certificates, a register of members inspection, and PPSR searches). Require a title warranty and fundamental warranty, uncapped or capped at price, with the Seller covering any title defect.

**18. Funds flow and price mechanics**
The funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics", but it excludes the bonuses, does not clearly show the Riverlark payoff, and does not clearly reflect debt-like items. For a debt-free, cash-free deal, the price adjustment mechanism (completion accounts, locked box, or price adjustment) needs to be clear.
*Push back:* Require a full, reconciled funds flow with every debt-like item, the Riverlark payoff, and a defined net debt and working capital mechanism. Confirm whether the deal is completion accounts or locked box, and confirm the leakage protections if it is locked box.

**19. Disclosure letter drafting issues**
Schedule numbering appears inconsistent (for example, the general disclosure is in Schedule 7 but the incident is in Schedule 6, and clause references are cross-referenced in different places). The DL also states that the Seller "does NOT" characterise several matters as confirmed (privacy incident, lease, Mossvale), which is helpful for the Buyer's argument that those matters are not disclosed as resolved.
*Push back:* Conform the schedule numbering and cross-references, and ensure that no general or non-admission language undermines the specific warranties.
